text: For a user-facing service, monitor latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
Measure latency for successful and failed requests separately; fast failures can make an overall latency measure look better while users still experience errors.
Track the resource most likely to constrain the service. Performance may degrade before that resource reaches its maximum, so define an appropriate operating target or early-warning level.
During overload, a lower-cost or less detailed response may reduce service work while preserving useful functionality, when that response is safe for the request.
Retries can increase traffic during overload. A retry budget limits the additional work caused by retries.
One Google SRE system example uses a per-request limit of three attempts and a per-client retry ratio below 10 percent. These are example settings, not universal defaults.
scope: Google SRE example, not a universal recommendation

text: When a lower-level service rejects a request because it is overloaded, the layer directly above it should own the retry decision; retries at several layers can multiply.
During an incident, reduce ongoing user impact and restore service; preserve useful evidence for later investigation.
The incident commander coordinates the overall response, maintains a shared view of the incident, assigns responsibilities, and removes blockers.
The operations lead coordinates technical mitigation and recovery. The operations team should be the group changing the affected production system during the incident.
The communications lead sends regular updates to responders and stakeholders, handles incoming questions, and keeps the incident record current.
Planning support can track longer-running work, resource needs, handoffs, and follow-up actions during a larger incident.
Maintain a shared, live incident record of impact, known facts, decisions, actions, and owners to coordinate responders and support later review.
For an incident-command handoff, brief the incoming commander and get clear acknowledgment before the outgoing commander steps away.
A service level objective (SLO) is a target for a user-relevant aspect of service reliability. Teams use SLOs to make informed reliability and product decisions.
A service level indicator (SLI) measures a user-relevant outcome. A common form is good events divided by total events, such as successful requests divided by all requests.
Start SLI and SLO design from the service and its users: identify important user journeys, choose a small set of measurable indicators, and refine them as you learn.
For a percentage-based SLO, the error budget is 100% minus the SLO. A 99.9% SLO leaves a 0.1% error budget.

One published Google SRE example policy pauses most changes and releases if the service exceeds its error budget over a four-week window, while allowing P0 issues and security fixes. This is an example, not a universal default.
One published Google SRE example policy requires a postmortem if a single incident consumes more than 20% of the four-week error budget. This threshold is specific to that example policy.
Error budgets help teams balance reliability and the pace of product changes, using reliability data to guide decisions about where to focus work.
A canary is a partial, time-limited deployment of a change that is evaluated before deciding whether to continue the rollout. The changed portion is the canary; the unchanged portion is the control.

A canary process needs a way to expose a subset of production to a change, an evaluation that classifies the change as acceptable or problematic, and integration of that evaluation into the release process.
Break evaluation metrics down by canary and control. Whole-service metrics can hide defects when only a small share of traffic reaches the changed version.
Start canary evaluation with user-impact indicators such as request errors and latency. Keep the metric set manageable and focused; weakly related or noisy signals can create false alarms.
If a canary performs worse than the control on important signals, pause the rollout and investigate or roll it back. If signals are acceptably similar, continue according to the release process.
Choose a canary size and duration that provide representative traffic and enough time for relevant problems to appear. Consider request diversity, traffic volume, time of day, and service behavior.
Use evaluation metric intervals that are no longer than the canary duration; longer aggregation windows can mix unrelated events into the comparison.
section: Match Metric Windows to the Canary
